data.summary:
Input: Sequence of operations including constructor, push, pop, top, and getMin.
Output: Results of the respective stack operations, with null for void methods.
Rules: All operations must run in O(1) time complexity.
constraints: Methods pop, top and getMin operations will always be called on non-empty stacks
At most 3 * 10^4 calls will be made to push, pop, top, and getMin

steps.title: Initialize Data Structures
steps.detail: Create two empty lists: `self.stack` to store all elements and `self.min_stack` to store the minimum elements.

steps.title: Push Operation
steps.detail: Push the value onto `self.stack`. For `self.min_stack`, push the new value if `self.min_stack` is empty or if the value is less than or equal to the current minimum.

steps.title: Pop Operation
steps.detail: Pop from `self.stack`. If the popped value equals the top of `self.min_stack`, also pop from `self.min_stack`.

data.generator_code:
import random

def generate(rng, n):
    ops = ["MinStack"]
    args = [[]]
    for _ in range(n):
        val = rng.randint(-10, 10)
        ops.append("push")
        args.append([val])
    return [ops, args]

def generate_worst(rng, n):
    ops = ["MinStack"]
    args = [[]]
    for i in range(n):
        ops.append("push")
        args.append([i])
    for _ in range(n // 2):
        ops.append("getMin")
        args.append([])
    return [ops, args]

data.pattern_summary: Maintain a secondary data structure alongside the main one to track state changes dynamically, avoiding redundant scans.

pattern_options.name: Two Stacks
pattern_options.feedback: Correct. Using an auxiliary stack to track the minimum alongside the main stack allows O(1) access.

pattern_options.name: Hash map lookup
pattern_options.feedback: Incorrect. A hash map does not preserve order and cannot easily track which minimum corresponds to the current state of the stack after pops.

pattern_options.name: Sorting
pattern_options.feedback: Incorrect. Sorting disrupts the LIFO order required by a stack.

pattern_options.name: Two pointers
pattern_options.feedback: Incorrect. Two pointers are used for sequential range traversal, not for tracking structural operations in a stack.

signals.hint: Implies you need a way to retrieve the minimum value efficiently without searching every time.

signals.phrase: All operations must run in O(1) time complexity.
signals.hint: Rules out any approach like looping that depends on the size of the stack.

data.brute_force_idea: Store all pushed elements in a single list acting as a stack. For push, pop, and top, simply use list operations. For getMin, iterate through the entire stack to find the smallest element.
data.brute_force_why: The getMin method iterates through all elements in the stack, taking time proportional to the number of elements.
data.bottleneck: Iterating through the entire stack every time getMin is called causes linear time complexity instead of constant time.
bottleneck_hints: Look at how getMin finds the minimum value.
Consider what happens to the minimum value when new elements are pushed or popped.
Can you store the minimum value alongside the data as it comes in so you never have to search for it?

data.overview: The MinStack data structure supports standard stack operations alongside a getMin operation, all in O(1) time. It achieves this by maintaining a secondary stack that tracks the minimum value corresponding to each element in the main stack.
data.intuition: Imagine a stack of plates where each plate has a sticky note showing the minimum weight of all plates at or below it. When you add a lighter plate, you add a new note; when you remove it, the note goes away too.

pitfalls: Using strict inequality (<) instead of non-strict (<=) when pushing to min_stack, which causes duplicate minimums to fail on pop.
Forgetting to pop from min_stack when the popped value from the main stack matches the current minimum.
Not handling empty stack scenarios if constraints did not guarantee non-empty calls.

data.insight: The brute force solution wastes time in getMin by rescanning the entire stack to find the minimum value. The optimized approach removes this bottleneck by maintaining a secondary stack (min_stack) that tracks the minimum value at each depth, allowing getMin, push, and pop to run in constant time.

derivation.note: Appending to the main stack runs once per push operation.
Checking the condition against the top of min_stack runs once per push.
Appending to min_stack occurs only when a new minimum is found.
Returning the top of min_stack takes direct constant time.

data.time_summary: Each method (push, pop, top, getMin) performs a constant number of O(1) list operations, resulting in O(1) time complexity per operation. Measured data confirms linear growth with respect to the total number of operations.
data.space_summary: The space complexity is O(n) because in the worst-case scenario (strictly decreasing elements), every pushed element is also pushed onto the min_stack, scaling linearly with the number of elements.
data.takeaway: When an operation requires tracking a running aggregate (like a minimum or maximum) alongside standard LIFO behavior, maintain a auxiliary data structure synchronized with the primary collection to cache state.
mistakes: Using strict inequality (val < min_stack[-1]) during push, which fails to track duplicate minimum values correctly.
Forgetting to pop from the min_stack when the popped element from the main stack matches the current minimum.
Attempting to update min_stack during getMin instead of during push and pop, which ruins the O(1) time requirement.
